pattern_title: CA rare catastrophic and unclassifiable inpatient outliers
pattern_description: CA cost growth is being driven by a concentrated set of rare, very high-cost inpatient cases rather than a broad-based clinical trend. Much of the impact sits in unclassifiable or highly unusual admissions, with several individual episodes carrying extremely high paid amounts. This should be treated as a case-level catastrophic outlier pattern first, not as general utilization growth.

summary_table.subtitle: CA rare catastrophic and unclassifiable inpatient outliers

claims.summary: CA rare and unclassifiable clinical cases added about +$16.0M. Three unclassifiable diagnoses alone contributed about +$7.2M: cervical cord lesion at C2 +$2.7M, other cirrhosis of liver +$2.6M, and dilated cardiomyopathy +$1.9M. Several admissions carried extremely high paid per admit, including a heart transplant or heart assist episode at HILLCREST MEDICAL CENTER of about +$1.4M.

pattern_title: CA acute hospital spend is rising through both provider mix and authorization mix
pattern_description: CA acute hospital cost growth is showing up across both PPO and HMO, with authorized admissions carrying most of the dollars. The increase is coming from a mix of more admissions at O'CONNOR HOSPITAL and higher paid per admit at HILLCREST MEDICAL CENTER and other concentrated providers. This is a provider-mix and authorization-mix problem, not a single-product issue.

summary_table.title: Payer Policy Summary
summary_table.subtitle: CA acute hospital spend is rising through both provider mix and authorization mix

claims.summary: CA PPO acute hospital authorized admissions added about +$5.8M, with 18 more admissions and paid per admit up about $81.1K. CA HMO acute hospital added about +$1.8M, concentrated at HILLCREST MEDICAL CENTER with 12 more admissions and paid per admit up about $118.3K. O'CONNOR HOSPITAL drove about +$1.2M across PPO and HMO through 35 more admissions even as paid per admit fell. Separate unit-cost-only pressure added about +$1.3M in CA acute hospital across PPO and HMO despite flat or lower admissions.

pattern_title: CA authorization-code movement must be validated before policy action
pattern_description: A material share of CA cost movement is tied to authorization-code distribution rather than a clear change in utilization or reimbursement. That means the first question is whether PA-required status, claim mapping, or classification changed. Business action on UM or reimbursement should wait until that mapping is reconciled.

pattern_title: Post-acute inpatient settings are a major site-of-care cost driver
pattern_description: Post-acute inpatient settings are producing a sizable share of the cost increase, especially LONG TERM CARE HOSPITAL and Physical Rehab. The pattern reflects both more admissions and very high paid amounts per admit, with several episodes concentrated in aftercare and unclassifiable cases. This is a site-of-care and level-of-care management issue more than a broad acute hospital trend.

pattern_title: Authorized PPO acute hospital pressure is recurring across multiple states
pattern_description: Authorized PPO acute hospital spend is not isolated to one market. Across the listed states, the pattern shows recurring pressure from cervical spine, aftercare, and unclassifiable admissions, with both more admissions and higher paid per admit. OH adds a separate unit-cost-led PPO acute signal even with fewer admissions.

pattern_title: NY cervical spine episodes are driving both clinical and operational growth
pattern_description: NY is showing a focused cervical spine pattern that appears in both clinical and operational views. Admissions are up for cervical spinal stenosis and cervical radiculopathy, and EPO acute hospital spend is rising on the same surgical family. This looks like a true specialty trend that should be managed at the episode level.

summary_table.title: Payer Policy Summary
summary_table.subtitle: NY cervical spine episodes are driving both clinical and operational growth

rows.policy_scope: Ambulatory surgical grouper policy paying surgery, including cervical spine fusion, under specified revenue code rules.

individual_policies.evidence: The policy is an ambulatory surgical grouper policy, not a DRG policy. It does, however, include cervical spine fusion CPT codes that are assigned grouper levels and are paid as surgical services when billed under the stated revenue code rules. No prior authorization, documentation, or diagnosis-specific exclusion is stated for these cervical fusion codes.

claims.summary: NY cervical spine-related clinical and operational patterns added about +$4.5M. Clinical cervical spinal stenosis added about +$2.2M with 22 more admissions, and cervical radiculopathy added about +$0.8M with 10 more admissions. NY EPO acute hospital cervical spinal fusion added about +$1.0M with 11 more admissions and paid per admit up about $27.4K. Aftercare with CC/MCC added another about +$0.5M in NY EPO acute hospital.

pattern_title: Small-volume provider and facility outliers are emerging outside the main markets
pattern_description: Several smaller providers and facility types are showing emerging cost signals that are individually small but collectively meaningful. The pattern is concentrated in CHILDRENS, CRITICAL ACCESS, and low-volume acute providers, often tied to rare cases or a handful of additional admissions. These are better handled through targeted exception review than through broad policy changes.

pattern_title: CA lower-acuity spine and aftercare episodes are rising in a focused cluster

The increase is concentrated in a limited set of diagnoses tied to aftercare and lumbar spine conditions rather than broad inpatient growth. This is best managed as an episode-pattern review.
